headline: Steam hardware breach leaks customer names and addresses in Europe
summary: Valve's European shipping partner, CEVA Logistics, experienced a data breach between July 29th and August 1st, potentially exposing customer information.
details: Valve has confirmed that a data breach at its European shipping partner, CEVA Logistics, may have exposed personal information of customers who ordered Steam hardware.

The incident, which occurred between July 29th and August 1st, could include customer names, addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses. This comes weeks after Valve began taking reservations for its new Steam Machine and Steam Controller.

Valve warns users to "expect fake messages" via email, text, or phone that impersonate Steam or delivery companies. These scams may quote personal details to appear legitimate and could ask for confirmation of delivery, payment of fees, or login verification.

The company assures that additional data linked to Steam accounts or purchases, such as payment information, passwords, or Steam Guard codes, was not impacted. CEVA Logistics does not have access to this sensitive data.

Valve emphasizes that it only handles account issues through help.steampowered.com and will not contact users via email, Steam chat, or Discord. Users are advised to treat all unsolicited communications as fake.

headline: AI data center bans surge past 500 nationwide as US politicians block new developments
summary: Growing public outrage and bipartisan pushback threaten big tech expansion plans, with over 500 local US politicians blocking new data center construction.
details: The number of local bans on new data center developments has surged past 500 in the United States, posing a significant threat to the expansion plans of AI firms. This trend is driven by growing public concern over the impact of these facilities on local communities, including noise pollution and strain on public services like water and electricity.

Analysis from The Information reveals that this is not a partisan issue, with both Republican- and Democrat-run states and towns enacting bans. Texas and New York are prominent examples, with the majority of moratoriums appearing in the Midwest and South.

Texas Governor Greg Abbott recently placed a moratorium on data center approvals pending an audit of companies connecting to the state's power grid. Despite this, Amazon plans to build a new gas power plant in Pecos County, Texas, to power a data center, a location already projected to be a major source of pollution.

The rapid growth of data centers has fueled resident concerns, with Florida and Georgia seeing a significant increase in moratoriums, particularly in July. Florida has 14 out of 23 active restrictions approved last month, with 15 more under consideration.

States like New York, Massachusetts, and Nebraska are also implementing measures. Governor Kathy Hochul of New York signed an executive order pausing approvals for data centers consuming 50 megawatts or more, while Massachusetts and Nebraska halted tax breaks for developers.

In Colorado, 19 bans are in place around Denver due to environmental and water usage concerns. Nashville, Tennessee, is also facing resistance for a $700 million data center development planned next to a zoo.

Public sentiment appears to be turning against the proliferation of AI data centers, with over 70% of Americans reportedly against new developments. Direct protests have also occurred, leading to at least 37 arrests this year.
